What we assumed, what we found, and what you should know

We set out to document a gap in medical education. The problem is real — but different from what most people assume going in. Here's what we found, including where we were wrong.

A note on scope. This is a student research project — two expert interviews, a review of available resources, and published literature. Our conclusions are a starting point for future inquiry, not a definitive answer. We've tried to be clear about what's well-established versus what's anecdotal.

University of Texas at Austin Health Outcomes / AI / Ethics · Spring 2026

01 — The problem

The stakes are real — and so is the debate about causes

Black patients with melanoma have a 5-year survival rate of 71%, compared to 94% for White patients. They are also more than three times as likely to be diagnosed at a late stage. These disparities are well-documented across national cancer registries and aren't disputed by researchers.

What is debated is why — and more importantly, what the most effective interventions are. Representation in medical education is one piece of a larger puzzle that includes healthcare access, provider distribution, patient awareness, and socioeconomic factors. We think the education piece is often framed in a way that sends well-meaning researchers toward solutions that don't address the real bottleneck.

Availability vs. integration: a critical distinction

A textbook available on Amazon is not the same as a required course text. An image dataset accessible online is not the same as a case shown during lecture. Keeping this distinction in mind is important as you read through what we found.

02 — Resources that already exist

Specialized resources exist — but knowing about them matters

When students and organizations discover the disparity data, the instinct is often to create something new — a database, a textbook, a repository. Our research suggests there's a more immediate step: the resources for dermatology in skin of color already exist, and many people simply don't know where to find them.

The resources below are vetted and real. Whether they're consistently integrated into medical school curricula is a separate, harder question — and one that still needs more research.

"Books exist. We don't need more. We need people to point to what is there."

03 — A perspective from the field

Dr. Adewole Adamson: the emails keep coming

AA
Adewole (Ade) Adamson, MD, MPP
Board-certified dermatologist · Assistant Professor, Division of Dermatology, Dell Medical School, UT Austin · Director, Melanoma and Pigmented Lesion Clinic, Dell Seton Medical Center · Published in NEJM, JAMA, JAMA Oncology, JAMA Dermatology
adeadamson.com ↗

Dr. Adamson — a Black dermatologist and researcher at Dell Medical School — regularly receives emails from medical students and student organizations who have discovered the melanoma disparity data and want to solve it. Their proposed solution is almost always the same: create something new.

His response is consistent: the resources already exist. He directs inquirers to the textbooks and datasets listed in Section 02. The problem, in his view, is not that dark skin images are absent from medical education — it is that students and generalist physicians are not being pointed to resources that are already there.

If you're here to solve this problem

Start with the resources in Section 02. Then ask a harder question: which of those are actually making it into the curricula that medical students and primary care physicians go through? That's where the real work is.

04 — What we found

The narrative is more complicated than the headline

We talked to dermatologists, educators, and researchers, and dug into the published literature. Some widely-repeated claims held up. Some didn't. Some of our own assumptions turned out to be wrong too. Here's what we found.

Reframing needed

"Dark skin images don't exist in medical education"

High-quality, vetted resources dedicated to skin of color do exist — see Section 02. But the STAR-ED study found only 10.5% dark skin representation across four commonly used dermatology textbooks,[1] and Perlman et al. (2021) found just 14.9% skin-of-color images across six popular medical student study tools — Amboss, First Aid, Pathoma, and others.[10] Specialized atlases exist. The materials most students are actually studying from tell a different story.

Confirmed

Dermatologists know what they're doing

Every dermatologist we spoke with felt confident and well-trained across the full range of skin tones — and that tracks with how the specialty works. Dermatology residency is a rigorous, clinically intensive training path. By the time someone is a licensed dermatologist, they've seen a wide breadth of presentations. The representation gap is not a dermatology problem. It lives upstream, in the general medical education that most doctors — and most patients — rely on long before they ever see a specialist.

Confirmed

Primary care training time is a critical bottleneck

Half of U.S. medical schools require 10 or fewer total hours of dermatology instruction, and 8% require none at all.[11] Meanwhile, roughly 90% of patients who need a skin evaluation see a primary care physician, not a dermatologist.[2] Even perfect resources can't help if there's no time to teach them.

Confirmed

Medical students report low confidence diagnosing skin conditions in darker skin

A Wayne State University study found that 89% of medical students felt "slightly confident or not confident at all" diagnosing skin diseases. When a supplemental skin-of-color module was added, confidence in diagnosing conditions on darker skin improved significantly.[14] It's not just about what resources exist — it's about what students are actually exposed to.

Confirmed

Online and general database images are often clinically inaccurate

Clinician educators were consistent on this: images from general internet searches and unvetted databases are frequently mislabeled or clinically inaccurate. The AAD and peer-reviewed journals are the trustworthy sources. More images isn't the answer — better curation of what already exists is.

Context needed

Who is raising this concern?

Some clinicians noted that students raising this issue may not have encountered the full specialist training pipeline yet — which is a fair point. But the published literature making the same argument was written by dermatologists and medical educators, not students. The concern has peer-reviewed backing.

06 — Interview notes

What we heard in the field

Below are distilled notes from two conversations that shaped our thinking — a researcher with an engineering lens, and a practicing dermatologist and educator. These are practitioner perspectives, not a representative sample.

AW
Alexander Whitman
Researcher — engineer perspective
Acknowledged the issue but noted that melanoma incidence is lower in people of color overall — likely the primary counterargument researchers will face from skeptics.
Proposed a more persuasive framing: "By including these images, we can intervene for X% of patients in this population."
Approached the problem from an engineering perspective — focused on diagnostic tools that perform well regardless of skin tone, a different intervention than educational materials.
Connected us to researchers publishing specifically on melanoma in skin of color.
JR
Jason Reichenburg
Dermatologist / Educator
Online and general database images are not clinically reliable — peer-reviewed journals and vetted clinical resources are the only trustworthy sources.
Medical schools allocate approximately 0–4 hours of skin-of-color-specific training — this figure comes from one educator's experience; published surveys report total dermatology hours of 10 or fewer at half of U.S. schools.[11]
Dermatologists are generally more aware of this problem than medical school educators.
Changing nursing school and medical school curricula may be more feasible than updating printed textbooks — the institutional inertia is lower.
Primary care physicians need better dermatology education far more urgently than dermatologists do.
Only about 10% of patients see a dermatologist. The diagnostic gap lives in primary care.
Databases or pamphlets may be more practical and higher-impact than new books or image repositories.

07 — Our prototype

What we built

These two flyers were created as a proof of concept — demonstrating that melanoma can and should be shown across all six Fitzpatrick skin types, and that the ABCDEs of melanoma apply regardless of skin tone. They are free to download and share.

Melanoma across all skin tones
Fitzpatrick types I–VI with clinical images and disparity statistics
